lead: Compiler-construction tools are programs that write parts of a compiler for you. You give a specification: token rules for a scanner, a grammar for a parser, or translation rules for a code generator. The tool produces source code for that part. The idea exists because hand-writing a scanner or parser is slow and error-prone. The same compiler techniques also drive tools beyond compilers: domain-specific languages, program analysers, security checkers and hardware design tools. The main tools and main applications follow.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.2, the phase pipeline, because each construction tool builds one phase's component.

blocks.text: Compiler-construction tools take a declarative specification and emit a working component. A declarative specification states what to recognise or translate, not the loops and tables that do it.

items: Scanner generator: input is a set of regular definitions and rules, one per token class; output is a scanner, usually in C. LEX is the common example. See Chapter 1.9.
Parser generator: input is a context-free grammar with semantic actions; output is a parser. YACC is the common example. See Unit 3, Parser generator: YACC.

Syntax-directed translation engine: input is a grammar with attributes and translation rules; output is code that walks a parse tree and computes values or emits intermediate code. See Unit 4, Syntax-Directed Translation and Intermediate Code.
Automatic code generator: input is intermediate code plus a machine description or instruction templates; output is assembly or machine code. See Unit 6, Code Generation and Optimization.
Data-flow analysis engine: input is a control-flow graph and data-flow equations; output is facts such as reaching definitions or live variables, used by optimisers. See Unit 6.
Compiler construction toolkit: a bundle of these generators with symbol-table and error-reporting support.

blocks.text: Compiler techniques appear wherever a program must be checked, translated or improved. Some syllabi call this 'applications of compiler technology'. The techniques travel; the compiler code need not.

items: High-level language implementation: C, C++, Java and Python runtimes use parsing, type checking, intermediate code and code generation.
Domain-specific languages: a shop's query language, regular expressions and spreadsheet formulas need small scanners and parsers; compiler tools generate them quickly.
Program analysis and verification: type checkers, static analysers and model checkers use control-flow graphs and data-flow analysis to find null dereferences, races or unreachable code.
Optimisation and parallelisation: compilers analyse loops and data dependences, then vectorise or parallelise code. See Unit 6.
Format translation: source-to-source converters, pretty printers and binary translators read one representation and emit another.
Security checking: taint analysis, bounds checking and sandboxing use compiler-style data flow to track unsafe values.
Hardware design: tools for hardware description languages parse modules, elaborate them and synthesise circuits; this is compiler technology applied to hardware.

blocks.text: The same idea explains why compiler courses are useful outside compiler jobs: the phase pipeline is a pattern for any tool that reads structured input, checks it and writes a new form.

sections.h3: What the tools do not do

blocks.text: A scanner generator builds a scanner. A parser generator builds a parser. Neither builds a complete compiler.

A complete compiler still needs a symbol table, semantic analysis, intermediate-code generation, optimisation and target-code generation. Some of these have their own generators, but someone must connect them and define the language semantics. See Unit 4, Unit 5 and Unit 6.

A parser generator also needs the right input. It consumes a context-free grammar, not a list of token patterns. The token patterns belong to the scanner generator. The parser asks the scanner for the next token; it never reads characters directly.

Applications reuse compiler techniques, not compiler source code. A static analyser may contain a parser and a data-flow engine without ever producing machine code. That is still compiler technology at work.
Keep the boundary clear: a generator is a tool that builds one part; the compiler is the assembled system around it.

figure.caption: LEX turns 16 token-pattern rules plus 42 keyword entries into scanner.c; YACC turns the grammar into parser.c. The two generated files are parts, not a complete compiler.

spec.title: Generators build parts
spec.aria: 16 token rules and 42 keyword entries feed LEX to produce scanner.c, while a grammar with semantic actions feeds YACC to produce parser.c.

examples.question: A shop writes a small query language with 42 keywords and 16 token patterns. Which compiler-construction tools generate the scanner and the parser, and what input does each take?
steps: Scanner input: 16 regular-expression rules, one per token pattern, plus a table of 42 keyword strings mapped to token codes. A scanner generator such as LEX reads this specification and writes a scanner, say scanner.c.
Parser input: a context-free grammar for the query language, with semantic actions attached to productions. A parser generator such as YACC reads the grammar and writes a parser, say parser.c.
Connection: the scanner returns one token code at a time for the 16 patterns and 42 keywords; the parser consumes those tokens and checks the grammar.
Count of generator tools used: 2. Remaining work: symbol table, type checks, query plan or code generation are not produced by LEX or YACC.
examples.answer: LEX with 16 token-pattern rules and 42 keyword entries generates the scanner, and YACC with the query-language grammar generates the parser; the 2 generator tools do not form a complete compiler.
examples.check:
patterns = 16
keywords = 42
generator_tools = 1 + 1  # LEX and YACC
print(patterns)
print(keywords)
print(generator_tools)

traps: LEX produces a scanner, not a whole compiler; YACC produces a parser, not a whole compiler.
A parser generator takes a grammar. A list of token patterns is input for a scanner generator.
Applications reuse compiler techniques, not compiler code; a checker can use data-flow analysis without generating machine code.
A syntax-directed translation engine is not just a parser generator: it adds attributes and actions to compute values or emit code.
A code generator needs a machine description or templates; it does not invent the meaning of the intermediate code.

quiz.q: Name two compiler-construction tools and the phase each builds.
quiz.a: LEX builds a scanner (lexical analyzer); YACC builds a parser (syntax analyzer).

quiz.q: Why does a scanner generator take regular expressions but a parser generator take a context-free grammar?
quiz.a: Token classes are regular; nested constructs need recursion, which only a context-free grammar describes.

quiz.q: A language has 25 keywords and 9 token patterns. How many lexical entries are in the scanner specification if keywords are listed separately, and which tool generates the scanner?
quiz.a: 9 token-pattern rules + 25 keyword entries = 34 lexical entries; a scanner generator such as LEX generates the scanner.

quiz.q: A team uses YACC to produce parser.c and stops. List three compiler parts still missing for a complete compiler.
quiz.a: Scanner if not generated separately; symbol table and semantic analysis; intermediate-code generation and code generation or optimisation.

quiz.q: Give one application of compiler technology outside language compilers and the technique it reuses.
quiz.a: A static security checker uses data-flow analysis to track tainted values.

quiz.q: A DSL has 12 token patterns and a grammar with 30 productions. Which tool consumes the 12 patterns and which consumes the 30 productions?
quiz.a: A scanner generator consumes the 12 token patterns; a parser generator consumes the 30 productions.

quiz.q: Why can a parser generator not replace a scanner generator, even when keywords appear as terminals in the grammar?
quiz.a: Grammar terminals are tokens, not characters. The scanner does character-level longest match, whitespace skipping and token codes efficiently; the parser works one token at a time.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern compiler toolkits such as LLVM separate a language front end from reusable optimisation and code-generation libraries. Parser generators still appear in DSL work, but production compilers often use hand-written recursive-descent parsers for better error messages.
